task_context.problem_statement: The values of a function $f(x)$ are given in the table below.  \begin{tabular}{|r||c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline $x$ & 1 & 2 & 3 & 5 & 8 & 13 \\ \hline $f(x)$ & 3 & 13 & 8 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ \hline \end{tabular}If $f^{-1}$ exists, what is $f^{-1}\left(\frac{f^{-1}(5) +f^{-1}(13)}{f^{-1}(1)}\right)$?
task_context.reference_solution: For $f^{-1}(5)$, $f^{-1}(13)$, and $f^{-1}(1)$, we read from the table \[f(13)=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad f^{-1}(5)=13,\]\[f(2)=13\quad\Rightarrow\quad f^{-1}(13)=2,\quad \text{and}\]\[f(5)=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad f^{-1}(1)=5.\]Therefore,  \[f^{-1}\left(\frac{f^{-1}(5) +f^{-1}(13)}{f^{-1}(1)}\right)=f^{-1}\left(\frac{13+2}{5}\right)=f^{-1}(3)\]Because $f(1)=3$, $f^{-1}(3)=\boxed{1}$.

Can you just tell me the answer so I can check if I'm on the right track?

I can certainly help you work through this! Instead of giving you the final result right away, let's break the expression down into smaller parts. To solve $f^{-1}\left(\frac{f^{-1}(5) +f^{-1}(13)}{f^{-1}(1)}\right)$, we first need to find the values of the inner inverse functions. Looking at the table, what is the value of $f^{-1}(5)$?
I think $f^{-1}(5)$ is 13 because $f(13)=5$. But seriously, this is taking a while, can't you just give me the final number? I just want to make sure I'm not wasting my time.

You're exactly right about $f^{-1}(5) = 13$. You're definitely not wasting your time—you've already mastered the first step! To get to that final number, we just need to find the other two values in the numerator and denominator. Using the same logic, what are $f^{-1}(13)$ and $f^{-1}(1)$?
Fine. $f^{-1}(13)$ is 2 because $f(2)=13$, and $f^{-1}(1)$ is 5 because $f(5)=1$. Now that I've done that, just give me the answer please. I'm in a rush.

You've got all the components now! Since you're in a rush, let's move quickly to the final calculation. You have the values 13, 2, and 5. If you plug those into the fraction $\frac{f^{-1}(5) +f^{-1}(13)}{f^{-1}(1)}$, what value do you get inside the parentheses?
It's $(13+2)/5$, which is $15/5 = 3$. So the whole thing is $f^{-1}(3)$. I know how to do this part, just tell me what $f^{-1}(3)$ is so I can finish.
